source: Pourcel, Colas, Oudeyer (2026 v2) Self-Improving Language Models for Evolutionary Program Synthesis: ARC-AGI (SOAR)
finding: Gap 1. At an equal budget of 6,000 LLM calls, spending half on sampling and half on execution-guided repair beats spending all 6,000 on sampling, for every open model tested. Both beat one-shot by a large margin.
numbers: ARC-AGI public test, % solved, one-shot / Sample-6k / Sample&Refine-6k: Qwen2.5-Coder-14B 1.00 / 5.63 / 14.25; 32B 1.50 / 12.63 / 19.87; Qwen2.5-72B 1.75 / 12.88 / 25.25; Mistral-Large-2 2.50 / 18.50 / 25.62. GPT-4.1 one-shot 8.00; Claude-4-Sonnet 20.75; o3-mini 38.25. Final self-improved system 52%.
limits: Budget is counted in LLM calls, not tokens. Refinement calls are longer than sampling calls. Models are non-reasoning. Table rows for the 7B and closed models are partly blank in the text extraction, so only four clean rows are quoted. Majority voting over outputs is used for selection, not only example fit. Sample-and-test, not hypothesis-in-words.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a counted test plus repair step over plain resampling at equal calls. Does not show it at equal tokens or with a reasoning model.

source: Naik et al. (2026 v5) PBEBench: Multi-Step Programming by Examples Reasoning Benchmark
finding: Gap 1, 7. Models that use long chain-of-thought or test-time compute far outrun those that do not on multi-step rule induction. Even GPT-5 and gpt-oss-120b stay below 5% on hard long cascades. Scaling the thinking length beat scaling the number of samples for gpt-oss-120b at matched compute.
numbers: PBEBench-Lite pass@1 (%): Qwen3-32B 1.8 without CoT vs 41.9 with CoT; gpt-oss-20b 40.6; gpt-oss-120b 62.5; Claude-4-Sonnet 29.7 vs Claude-4-Sonnet Thinking 35.8; Claude-4-Opus Thinking 53.9; o3-mini 19.6; o4-mini 36.3; Gemini 2.5 Flash 58.6; GPT-5 72.4. Hard set: solve rate under 5% for GPT-5 and gpt-oss-120b even with big budgets.
quote: as heuristic proposal mechanisms that impose structure on the search space, motivating hybrid neuro-symbolic approaches
limits: Domain is string-rewrite cascades from historical linguistics, a narrow task type. The sampling-vs-thinking comparison is for one model (gpt-oss-120b), partly because that model wastes samples on unterminated chains. Accepts any candidate consistent with the examples, so the verifier is exact.
agent_relevance: Gives one direct matched-compute result: longer thinking beats more samples when single samples often fail to finish. Supports a hybrid: LLM proposes, exact checker verifies.

source: Naik et al. (2026 v5) PBEBench: scaling and wall effects
finding: Gap 7. Pass rate falls steadily with cascade length (the number of chained rules). Extra compute gives quick early gains, then diminishing returns and a wall. Adding more input-output examples per task slightly lowers accuracy. Many models cannot even order the correct rules when handed the right set (length 2 to 5).
numbers: Hypothesis space grows as O(|Sigma|^(2kL)) in cascade length L. Ordering-only variant has at most 4! = 24 valid orders for n<=5, yet accuracy still falls with length. GPT-5 at length 20 gets moderate accuracy with sampling budget 4; gpt-oss-120b near zero at length 20 even with sampling budget 32 and 16,384 tokens.
limits: Exact figures for the scaling curves are in an appendix that was not opened. Rules here interact by order (feeding, bleeding), which is stronger coupling than Gandarela's independent-predicate CHAIN.
agent_relevance: Chain-length cutoff is real. When a candidate rule set needs ordered interacting steps, expect single-LLM induction to break and hand to a search or solver.

source: Hua et al. (2025 v4) InductionBench: LLMs Fail in the Simplest Complexity Class
finding: Gap 4, 7. Even the best reasoning model barely induces the simplest function classes (subregular hierarchy), and success is scored as exact compatibility with all data.
numbers: Leaderboard (average, weighted toward hard settings): o3-mini recall 28.93, precision 43.12, compatibility 5.69%; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B compatibility 0.78%; Llama-3.3-70B 0.12%. With log weights o3-mini compatibility 33.93%, R1-Distill 8.63%. Zero-shot CoT at k=4, 3 rules: compatibility 0 for all but o3-mini.
limits: Task is a clean formal one (string maps with look-ahead window k). Compatibility is strict. o1 was not fully tested (restricted access). Table 1 rows lost model labels in extraction; only the leaderboard numbers are quoted.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models help but do not close the induction gap on formal rule classes. Plan for a verifier and a way to say 'not found'.

source: Hua et al. (2025 v4) InductionBench: few-shot and sample-size effects
finding: Gap 6. More in-context examples help only when the window k and vocabulary are small. As complexity grows, extra examples give negligible gain. Larger k sharply lowers recall, precision and compatibility for all models.
numbers: Llama-3.3-70B tested at 1, 2, 3 shots. Increasing k from 2 to 4 markedly reduces all three metrics for every model.
limits: Only Llama-3.3-70B was used for the few-shot test, so no result for reasoning models. Exact numbers in appendix tables not opened.
agent_relevance: Cheap predictor of refine-failure: hypothesis space size (window, vocabulary). If it is large, more examples or rounds may not help.

source: Parab et al. (2025) Analysis of Error Sources in LLM-based Hypothesis Search for Few-Shot Rule Induction
finding: Gap 2. Module-by-module analysis of Wang's hypothesis search on 100 list-function tasks with GPT-4o. The generator is the bottleneck: it produces a correct hypothesis in under half of 64-sample trials. The summariser then throws away 26% of the correct ones. Code writing with execution refinement rescues many wrong hypotheses.
numbers: 64 hypotheses per trial, summarised to 8. Generator 46.4% correct, summariser 34.5%, implementor 61.2%. Overall test solve rate 62.0%. Summariser keeps only 74% of correct generator hypotheses (12.1% absolute loss). If generator right and summariser wrong, implementor still correct 75.3%; if both right, 95.9%; implementor rescues 1,092 double-failure trials (19.9% of trials, 37.0% of the double-failure group). Trial-level correlation generator vs implementor r=0.57 (train), 0.55 (test); by task r=0.93 and 0.79. Up to 257 LLM calls per task.
limits: Single model (GPT-4o), one benchmark. A trial counts as success if at least one of 64 hypotheses is correct, a recall-at-64 style measure; no curve for smaller N in the text opened. 'Correct' is judged against a ground-truth description.
agent_relevance: Recall of a correct hypothesis at N=64 is about 46%; condensing candidates is a lossy selection step. Keep several raw candidates and test them on examples rather than trusting a summary.

source: Parab et al. (2025) Table 1 mean test accuracy
finding: Gap 1, 2. On the same 100 tasks hypothesis search roughly matches humans in mean test accuracy and beats direct program generation. It reaches more tasks than humans but its programs are more brittle.
numbers: Mean test accuracy: humans 0.521 (sd 0.202); Hypothesis Search 0.487 (sd 0.326); direct generation GPT-4o 0.359 (sd 0.309); Codex 0.322 (sd 0.467, from Rule et al.).
limits: Hypothesis search uses far more calls than direct generation, so this is not equal compute. Brittleness inflates sd.
agent_relevance: Confirms the Wang direction in a replication by a different team, but again not matched on tokens.

source: Li, Wang, Zheng, Song (2025) Patterns Over Principles: Fragility of Inductive Reasoning in LLMs under Noisy Observations
finding: Gap 3, 6. Robust Rule Induction task with 10% noisy examples across arithmetic bases, ciphers and list functions. Their SRR method (diverse example subsets plus execution feedback) loses least under noise. Accuracy can stay level while the model's answers on individual items flip, so rules are unstable. A reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1) is better but still not stable.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1, clean to 10% noise, task accuracy and consistency: Atbash CoT 65.0 to 65.0 (change 0.0), consistency 70.0; Atbash SRR 82.0 to 79.0, consistency 93.0; List Functions CoT 76.0 to 68.4 (-7.6), consistency 87.6; List Functions SRR 83.6 to 78.0 (-5.6), consistency 89.6. Abstract: 0% accuracy change with only 70% consistent score.
limits: Noise is random label replacement. No explicit length or MDL penalty; selection is by execution accuracy on examples. The main GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 table was garbled in extraction and is not quoted.
agent_relevance: A plain 'fit all examples' loop with a strong model loses 5 to 8 points at 10% noise. Argues for tolerating a few misfits instead of demanding perfect coverage.

source: Sharma, Dumancic, King, Cropper (2026 v2) Learning Logical Rules Using Minimum Message Length
finding: Gap 3. A Bayesian MML cost (hypothesis length plus data given hypothesis, with priors that favour general programs) is compared with the C-MDL cost used by MaxSynth on 30 datasets (Trains, Zendo, 1D-ARC, Alzheimer). Choosing among 10,000 random programs, MML and C-MDL pick equally accurate programs on ordinary and on 10-50% noisy data. MML wins when examples are few or one-sided.
numbers: Q1a (30 tasks): no significant difference MML vs C-MDL. Q1b (10-50% added noise and real Alzheimer data): no significant difference. Q2 (training sets of 20 and 50, positive:negative from 10:0 to 0:10): MML better in all 12 conditions, significant (p<0.05, Benjamini-Hochberg Wilcoxon) in 11 of 12. 10 repeats per task.
limits: No LLM is used; candidates are random programs or CP-SAT picks. Balanced test accuracy. Authors suspect their prior is too optimistic in noisy low-signal domains.
agent_relevance: Length-penalised scoring helps mainly when data are scarce or skewed, the agent's few-example setting. Not shown better than simple fit-minus-length under moderate noise. Still untested in an LLM loop.

source: Sharma et al. (2026 v2) MML paper: positive-only learning and design of selection
finding: Gap 3. The MML approximation can learn from exclusively positive examples, because the likelihood term penalises over-general programs. Plain consistency checks cannot do this.
numbers: Q5 uses APPROXLEARNER with CP-SAT, 180 s per call, 1000 s trial timeout, on noiseless tasks and positive-only or negative-only versions. Q3 uses training sizes 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500.
limits: The abstract claims significant outperformance on predictive accuracy; the text opened shows the margin is concentrated in unbalanced and small-data settings.
agent_relevance: If the agent can score a rule only against confirming cases, a generality penalty is needed or the model picks 'accept everything'.

source: Lin et al. (2025) On LLM-Based Scientific Inductive Reasoning Beyond Equations (SIRBench-V1)
finding: Gap 6. On real scientific tasks (molecules, reactions, DNA) hypothesis refinement gives little or no gain over writing a rule and answering in one pass, and sometimes hurts. The authors say refined rules were not always applied well, and the pick of the best hypothesis used only an automatic accuracy score that misses scientific plausibility.
numbers: Average accuracy: Gemini-2.5-Flash 43.81%, GPT-4.1 32.41%, Claude-3.5-Haiku 31.53%. With hypothesis refinement: Gemini 39.06%, GPT-4.1 33.25%, Haiku 31.63%. Refinement loop up to 3 rounds. Self-consistency used n=5.
limits: Non-reasoning models only. Tasks have fuzzy, domain-laden outputs so exact example fit is not a clean signal.
agent_relevance: Hint for a stop rule: do not refine when the check on examples is a weak proxy for correctness (perceptual or fuzzy outputs).

source: O'Brien, Haddow, Allaway, Chen (2025) MATHEMAGIC: Dynamic Mathematics Benchmarks Robust to Memorization
finding: Gap 4. In altered-arithmetic tasks, stating the rule in words beats 512 examples for small models, but the strongest reasoning model (GPT-5) learned from examples as well as from the stated rule. So the induce-versus-apply gap shrinks for current reasoning models on this task.
numbers: At 512 shots: GPT-4o-mini deductive (rule, zero-shot) 71.4% vs inductive 47.8%; GPT-5 inductive 87.2% vs zero-shot deductive 83.7%. Zero-shot baseline about 20% (answers right by chance via normal arithmetic). GPT-5 and GPT-5-nano rise with more examples and plateau near 32 shots. Nine transformations, five seeds.
limits: 'Induction' here is implicit: the model uses examples without writing the rule. It is not the MiniSCAN setup where the model writes a rule and then must apply it. Arithmetic only.
agent_relevance: Suggests the induce/apply gap is smaller for 2025-26 reasoning models, but the test differs from Qiu's. Keep a fresh apply step as a cheap check.

source: O'Brien et al. (2025) MATHEMAGIC: failure modes and fine-tuning
finding: Gap 4, 6. Small models revert to standard arithmetic. One model got worse with many examples. Fine-tuning on induction tasks transfers poorly.
numbers: Llama3 8B rose to 32.7% then fell sharply after 128 shots. Format errors drop from 64.0% at zero shots to 22.4% at 32 shots. Fine-tune gains up to +60.6% on a trained transformation (TRIG_S) but losses elsewhere, e.g. -21.4% (SWP_D); one test-set gain +55.1% exceeded the train gain +46.8%.
limits: Open models tested; fine-tuning is outside our no-training scope.
agent_relevance: More examples can hurt a weaker model, so cap example count and check for reversion to the default (prior) rule.

source: Singhal, Mishra, Malach, Galanti (2026 v3) LLM Priors for ERM over Programs (LLM-PV)
finding: Gap 2, 9. A propose-then-verify recipe with an LLM as sampler and held-out validation as the selector recovers exact rules from 200 labelled examples where trained transformers fail even with 100,000. Theory: the LLM need only put enough mass on a correct program so one appears in k tries.
numbers: m=200 examples split 100 train / 100 validation, test on 10,000. LLM-PV reaches 100% test accuracy on IsPrime with 200 examples; SGD transformers fail with 100k. Needed proposals k >= log(2/delta) / (-log(1 - p)), p being the proposal mass on good programs; uniform sampling would need about |Sigma|^L trials.
limits: Algorithmic tasks (parity, patterns, primality) with exact labels; no noise. The ChatGPT web trace is a case study. The bound gives k only in terms of p, which is unknown.
agent_relevance: Gives the formula for how many candidates are enough: k grows as 1/p. If p is 0.46 (Parab) a handful suffices; if p is 0.05, expect about 60.

source: Jiang, Yi, Zhu (2026) Sketch-and-Verify: Structured Inference-Time Scaling via Program Sketching
finding: Gap 2 (indirect). Diverse candidates beat more flat samples at matched count, because flat sampling duplicates answers. Verified by execution on tests (HumanEval+), not example induction.
numbers: Hard subset of 19 problems where Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite greedy fails: Sketch K=2,M=5 recovers 11/19 (58%) vs flat N=10 5/19 (26%); Sketch K=10,M=10 15/19 (79%) vs flat N=100 10/19 (53%); flat N=50 still loses to K=2,M=5 by 11 points. Pro greedy 89% beats Lite Sketch K=10,M=10 (79%) on pass@1 and dollars.
limits: Code generation with given tests, not rule induction. 19-problem subset, small model, single-lab preprint.
agent_relevance: Diversity of hypotheses matters more than count; recall-vs-N flattens on duplicates. A stronger model greedy can beat any amount of search on a weak one.

source: Muggleton, Schmid, Zeller, Tamaddoni-Nezhad, Besold (2018) Ultra-Strong ML: comprehensibility of programs learned with ILP, Experiment 2
finding: Gap 8. Human trial of Michie's ultra-strong criterion: can a machine-learned rule help a person do better than from examples alone? Almost no participant could write the target relational rule from examples. After seeing the rules Metagol learned, scores rose a lot.
numbers: Rule Acquisition and Application (RAA) group n=22; 13 tried to write rules, 11 in Prolog, and only 1 gave the correct rule. Scores of the other 21: first test mean 1.76 (sd 2.07), second test after seeing ILP rules mean 5.24 (sd 1.92), t(21)=7.63, p<0.001. Rule-application-only group (n=21) mean 4.33 (sd 2.39), difference not significant (W=267, p=0.119).
limits: Humans, not LLMs. Fictitious chemistry domain chosen so humans cannot induce it. No count of examples needed by Metagol is reported in the part opened.
agent_relevance: A rule written from examples can carry information the learner could not extract; supports having an inducer write the rule and a separate applier use it.

source: Muggleton et al. (2018) Ultra-Strong ML, Experiment 1 (predicate invention)
finding: Gap 8, 9. 78 analysed participants (of 87) read logic programs about family relations. Giving predicates meaningful names helped. Invented predicates helped only when they shortened the program, not in general.
numbers: Grandfather score: correct naming mean 6.68 (sd 0.61, n=28) vs incorrect 5.15 (sd 1.81, n=46) vs no answer 4.75 (n=4). Grandparent: 6.56 (n=50) vs 5.04 (n=23) vs 3.4 (n=5). ILP can generate rules meeting the ultra-strong criterion: confirmed; predicate invention helps comprehension: partially confirmed.
limits: Cognitive science students, mean age 23.55. Naming effects are correlational.
agent_relevance: Invented concepts should be named and kept short; opaque helpers cost comprehension.

source: Lin, Dechter, Ellis, Tenenbaum, Muggleton (2014) Bias reformulation for one-shot function induction (MetagolDF)
finding: Gap 8. One-shot induction of string-transformation programs: learning earlier tasks and reusing invented predicates makes later programs smaller, faster to find and more accurate. Accuracy from one example approaches FlashFill and humans.
numbers: 30 problems with 5 input-output examples each; 17 used in the human comparison; 85 train-test points (5 runs x 17). Train on 1 example, test on the other 4. Ten-minute cap per task, about one minute on average. 169 Mechanical Turk subjects: 87% accuracy on cyphered strings, 74% uncyphered; FlashFill 76% (less sensitive to the cypher). Non-recursive bias accuracy dropped only from 61.2% to 60.6%. A weaker bias reached around 40% with a monotonic rise over tasks.
limits: Problems were chosen to fit the system's primitives, so no general claim vs FlashFill. Per-task accuracy was read only from a figure description.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that few examples can be enough in symbolic induction, and for reusing earlier verified predicates (a rule library). One-shot learning depends on strong background knowledge.

source: Search log: LLM plus Popper-style constraints from failures (Gap 10)
finding: Gap 10. A targeted web search for papers that feed an LLM's own failed hypotheses into Popper-style constraints found none from 2025-2026. Only Popper and its follow-ups (e.g. MUSP constraints, 2401.16383) came up.
numbers: No numbers. One search, results not read in full.
limits: Absence in one search is weak evidence. ALBI and Reason Popper-ly (already in evidence_c) are the nearest hybrids.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: the agent-side test (forbid the failure class) has not been run by anyone we found.

source: Search log: wrong-rule propagation in rule stores, and open-domain predicate invention (Gaps 5, 9)
finding: Gaps 5, 9. Searches this round turned up no new study on wrong-rule propagation in an HtT-style store, nor any open-domain predicate-invention study with token cost. LLM-PV is a close cousin on the verify-before-keep side.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not read; absence from a few searches only.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 9 remain open; keep K11 and K14 single-source.
